utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, 25th of March, 2010. I would like, first of all, to greet the witness who is about to take the solemn declaration, I would like to greet the accused, the Defence counsel, all the members of the OTP, and all the people assisting us in this courtroom. I will first give the floor to the Registrar, who has two IC number to give to us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 2D has submitted its response to the Prosecution's objections to its documents tendered through Witness Milivoj Petkovic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01225. They have also submitted their objection to the Prosecution's list of documents tendered through Witness NO. This list shall be given Exhibit IC01226. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Witness, I would like you to stand, please. Can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Pero Nikolic. I was born on the 1st of November, 1944, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you read the solemn declaration, may I ask you whether you have testified before a court of law before or is this the first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down. You are a Defence witness of Mr. Coric. The Defence lawyer, whom you've met, I'm sure, has explained to you how things unfold here. She will put questions to you and she will show you a few documents. After that, the Defence counsel of the other accused may put questions to you as part of the time they have been allocated, and then the Prosecutor will have one hour to put questions to you as part of his cross-examination. And if necessary, the Judges on the Bench may also put questions to you. As far as possible, try and be accurate and succinct in the way you answer your questions. If there's a question you don't understand, please don't hesitate to ask for the question to be rephrased. I hope I have been clear enough. And without any more adieu, I shall give the floor to Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, whom I greet once again. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you too, sir. You'll be handed the documents in just a moment. You have pink stickers with the numbers of the documents, so please turn to document number 1, please, which is 5D05111. Tell me, Witness, is that your statement? You can look through it. You don't have to read through the whole of it. Just glance at it. You looked at it during the proofing session, so just have a look and tell me if your signature is on every page and if it is your statement.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement and it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, have you had an opportunity to read through your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Is there anything in that statement that you'd like to change now or add to?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by everything you said in the statement?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: If you were to be asked about the facts that you deal with in your statement, would your testimony be the same as it is in your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a few questions following your statement, so listen to me carefully, please. And before you give your answer, make a pause between my question and your answer so that we can allow the interpreters to interpret what we're saying. Mr. Nikolic, in your statement it says that on the 1st of May, 1992, you were appointed warden of the prison in Mostar, district prison in Mostar. Tell me, who appointed you to this position first?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was appointed by the Municipal Staff of the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that a civilian or a military prison?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was a civilian prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And what street was the prison in?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It was in Aleksa Santic Street, and that street was known as Ricina Street before.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us what the capacity of the prison was. How many prisoners or inmates could it hold?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The capacity of the prison was around 200 inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during 1992, while you were in prison, what category of inmates were there in the prison?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The category of persons coming to the prison was: civilians, military who had committed a criminal offence, and there were a few prisoners of war who were Serbs, but there was a small number of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, these POWs that you said were Serbs, I assume that they were soldiers belonging to the Army of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell us what the situation was like in the prison in the summer of 1992. What were the conditions? How many people were there and so on?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The conditions in the prison, in part, was good, for a time it was good, everything was in order, until people kept coming in on a daily basis, and more than more people came to the prison, so it was overcrowded. And then the conditions changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And when it became overcrowded, did you undertake anything?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I informed the Municipal Staff. They had a commission, and the commission called me up. Three Bosniaks and three Croats were the commission members. I told them that the prison was overcrowded, and that something should be done about it, and that the military -- that the military and civilian part should be separated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And did the commission take any steps?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The commission informed me subsequently that they had discussed the matter with the commander of the Heliodrom and that I was to report to him to see how things should be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: When you say the warden or the commander of Heliodrom, you mean the commander of the barracks of Heliodrom; right?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander of the Krusevac Battalion -- Mile Krusevac Battalion. Or, rather, his name was Milo Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you contact this man, Milo Pusic?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I contacted the person from the Main Staff, with Milo Pusic, and asked him to provide the necessary conditions for me to be able to put up the military detainees who had committed a criminal offence. So I went to see him, and he gave me one larger building and two smaller buildings. He placed them at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were those ready to take in the inmates?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, they hadn't been accommodated for that because they didn't have any bars for them to be kept inside. They belonged to the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did you or somebody else organise any construction work in those buildings then?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When I returned to Mostar, I contacted the company Sokol Mostar, which was a construction company, and I asked them to manufacture those bars so that the detainees could be placed in the prison, and it was a metal constructing company.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in charge of the construction work at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I didn't have time to go to Heliodrom or to follow the work, but I appointed Mr. Josip Praljak as my deputy in the prison because he is a construction technician, so I asked him to supervise the work done by the Sokol Mostar company.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, except for you and Mr. Josip Praljak, was anybody else in any way involved in the organisation of the construction work and supervision work?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, if you remember, when did the work end? When was everything completed?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what the date was, but sometime in August, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: 1992. I know that it was -- there was a heat wave, it was very hot.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And after the construction work was completed, did Heliodrom start working as a prison?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sometime in the autumn, the detainees -- military detainees were not coming in to Santic Street anymore, if there were any. I don't know exactly. I didn't go there anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, what happened to those who were with you, the military detainees and prisoners of war? Were they transferred to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Not all of them, no. There was the third floor for military detainees. They were independent -- alone there, without civilians. It was just them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And the majority were transferred; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the military prison system and organisation? Do you know which military prisons existed and how they functioned?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, no, I don't, because I'm a construction worker, I never worked in a military prison, so I really couldn't tell you what the structure and organisation of a military prison was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when Heliodrom started working, do you know who the prison warden of the Heliodrom was?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was Mile Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know who appointed him warden?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you were in the civilian prison for the whole of 1993, were you, in Santic Street?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I had a break. I wasn't there for 20 days, a period of 20 days, at one point.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, let's go back. You said that after they were transferred, there were POWs and military detainees still at Heliodrom. And as far as I understood it, in your prison there were civilians who had committed criminal offences, and on the third floor had you some of these military detainees?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me whether in any part of 1993 the rest of these military detainees were transferred to Heliodrom -- or from Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, because it's been 18 years since then.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the situation was like in Mostar after the 9th of May, after what happened on the 9th of May and what the situation was like?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There was shooting in Mostar, uncontrolled hoards, I would say, of people. There was no electricity -- there was no electricity in town. People were afraid to walk around at night in the dark.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, on the 9th of May, did a conflict and clash occur between the BH Army and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: After that clash, did those military detainees remain in your prison?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Until when? Were they transferred quickly after the conflict began or what?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now, tell us, the civilians, were they transferred to Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were transferred to Heliodrom together with the military detainees, because they were afraid of the shooting. They were under a mental shock. They were crying, they said they hadn't come there to be killed, to die, and about 10 of them went to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, a part of those civilians left in the first group, but did these military detainees leave with them?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The military detainees went with the army and the military policemen, and the military -- and the civilian detainees were transferred in vans with ordinary policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did they go all together?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In a column one after another, but on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, when this one group of civilians left -- you said that the civilian detainees left, a group who was afraid, and these military detainees left too. After that, did you have any more civilian detainees there?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, but a small number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now take a look at the last document that you have. It's P02925. Have you found it? It's the last document, and I'd like you to look at the penultimate page. Have you ever seen this document before? I showed it to you during the proofing session, but did you see it before that?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, never until last night.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this document, it says it's an order dated the 24th of June, which says that because of a war situation, prisoners shall be transferred to Heliodrom. And this was in June, the 24th of June. And a person named Zdenko Gavran is mentioned. Do you remember, were these people transferred, and do you remember somebody called Zdenko Gavran?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I do remember Zdenko Gavran, yes. I remember that particular moment. It was in the afternoon, when the 2nd Battalion, headed by Mr. Zdenko Gavran --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Just tell me whether -- the remainder of your civilian detainees, were they transferred?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, after they were transferred, and at that moment you didn't have any detainees, was your prison still operational, was it still working?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: For how long did it not work?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: For some 10 or 20 days, not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And after the 10 or 20 days, did you return?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I returned because I was forbidden to enter the prison, but then I returned. The judiciary gave me a decision, ordering me to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, the prison started functioning again?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now I'm just going to ask you briefly: Do you know Mr. Josip Praljak?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course I do, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: For how long have you known him, since when?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I first met him in 1972. He was my colleague. At that time, I was the chief of the prison in Mostar. I was given a residence from my former company, and then I recommended him to replace me.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: What is your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: My relationship with him is good. I was -- I even godfathered his children, and about a month ago I attended his son's wedding.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Valentin Coric? Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Valentin Coric was a karate champion of Yugoslavia. I may be mistaken. He is a great athlete, and I know that he was the chief of the military police. That's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever meet Mr. Coric? Did you socialise with him?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. He was not my superior, so there was no need for me to meet with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever meet not just as your superior, but in any other capacity?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever attend a meeting which was attended also by Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the second document in the binder. I showed you the document during the proofing session. P00352 is the number of the document. Look at page 12 in that document. And in the English version, it is page 11.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. What number?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Page 12. There are numbers, "0354-0181," in the upper right-hand corner. Were you able to find it, sir?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: 3545081 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I showed you this document during the proofing session. This is Mr. Josip Praljak's diary or an excerpt from him diary. Did you know that Mr. Josip Praljak wrote a diary?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the page in front of you, and on the upper right-hand side corner, it says "A meeting with warden." The date is 17 August 1992, and it says here: "Warden informed me he had announced a meeting with Valentin Coric in Ljubuski." And now turn to the following page, please, the annotation for the 8th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise to my learned colleague to interrupt. Perhaps just to assist her, I think that the entry she was looking at was not the 17th of August, but I think to the right of that entry the date says the 7th of September, if I'm not mistaken. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend. It is my mistake. The contents are not in dispute. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Turn to the following page. The entry is for the 8th of September, 1992, and it says here --

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't find the date. What date was that?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: 8th of September, the following page, the one after the one that you have just looked at.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The 7th?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, the 8th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: It says here "Meeting in Ljubuski with Chief Valentin Coric." And it says here that in addition to Mr. Coric, the meeting was attended by yourself and Mr. Josip Praljak. Did you ever attend that meeting? Were you aware of that meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Josip Praljak ever tell you that he had attended a meeting with Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Josip Praljak ever mention Mr. Coric?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: How often did you meet with Mr. Praljak in 1992 and 1993? We hear that you still maintained very good relations. How often do you see him?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Recently, I don't see him -- I have not seen him that often. But earlier on, he did come to the prison. But now we don't see each other that often. I have my job, he has his own. Perhaps he's even retired. I didn't ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, did you visit each other in your homes?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, we did not visit each other in our houses because there were no houses, there was no room to entertain anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. I just want to avoid any misunderstanding. Witness, you have first told us that you were a pensioner, when asked about your occupation. Just now, you have said "he had his job and I had my job." Could you explain why you are a pensioner, but also you have a job, and what is the job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1994, Your Honours, I opened my own business, a shop. The name of the shop is "Nik," and it consists of a shop and building operations. And before -- until two years ago, I was in charge of one part of that job, and then I handed it over to my wife. And then after 40-odd years, the time has come for me to retire, and then I retired two years ago, after having run that shop and that construction business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 13 of your statement - you can look at it, please - you said that you can safely assert that Mr. Valentin -- or, rather, that Mr. Praljak never mentioned to you that Mr. Valentin Coric had any role in appointing him or anybody else at Heliodrom. Tell me, please, during that period of time in 1992 and 1993, did Mr. Praljak talk to you about appointments at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did talk to me about that. He wanted to be warden himself because he thought that he had the knowledge and ability, and I never heard him mention Mr. Valentin Coric. And he asked me who he should turn to in order to land that appointment, and then I sent him to the Crisis Staff of the city of Mostar. I told him that he knew those men himself. He could write to them, he could talk to them in person, and he could ask them. He could inquire about the job.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did he do that?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not have any feedback from him. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. For Mr. Pusic's Defence, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 1D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom, and good morning, sir. We have no questions for the gentleman, but we do wish to thank him for coming here to give his evidence. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. The Stojic Defence does not have any questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. 3D does not have any questions for this witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to finish, 4D.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning to you and to everybody in the courtroom. Mr. Nikolic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Petkovic Defence, I'm going to have a few questions for you. I wish to have clarification of some parts of your statement. Please listen to me carefully, and if you don't understand something in my question, please tell me that you don't. Just a moment. Let me get things organised here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 7 of your statement, Mr. Nikolic, which you confirmed earlier today while talking to Ms. Tomasegovic, you said that Mile Pusic, who was the commander of the Krusevo Battalion and also the commander of the Heliodrom Barracks, gave the Municipal Staff permission to use one bigger building and two smaller buildings in the Heliodrom and turn them into a military prison; is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, tell us, please, if you know, who was the owner of all the buildings at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before the war, it was the JNA, and it used to be a military school.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And when the war started in the area of Mostar and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who was the owner then?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The HVO conquered it, together with all the other buildings, and the 7th Krusevac Battalion was billeted there. And as for the owner, I really don't know. I don't know what is written in the paperwork.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: P424 is the next document I would like you to look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, P424. This is a decree on the take-over of equipment from the JNA and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, and the reassignment of property to Herceg-Bosna. Article 1 says that: "The socially-owned resources on the territory of the HZ-HB, which is property of the Federation, is managed and used by the Yugoslav People's Army and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence shall become the property of the HZ-HB." A special reference is made to real estate, including buildings at Heliodrom. In Article 5 of this decree, it is stated: "The head of the Defence Department is hereby authorised to appoint the management bodies of institutions after first obtaining the opinion of the ministry under whose jurisdiction the activity of the institution falls. He shall also appoint and dismiss the management. The supervision of the professional work and the legality of the work of the institution stipulated in Article 3 of this decree shall be carried out by the ministries under whose jurisdiction the activities of the institutions fall." Witness, do you know that everything that was property of the JNA and the Federal Secretariat of National Defence in mid-1992 were proclaimed property of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the following document, which is P452. This is a decision of the head of the Defence Department, dated 3rd September 1992, and he refers to the decree on treating persons captured in armed conflicts in HZ-HB. He issues the decision on the establishment of the Central Military Prison at Heliodrom, and under number 2 he appoints Mile Pusic warden of the Central Military Prison. Mr. Nikolic, is that the same Mile Pusic that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the statements of reason accompanying this decision, it is stated that the decision was issued upon the proposal of the head of the Department of Justice and Administration and in connection with a real need to separate the military prison in Mostar after it has been established that the premises, pursuant to Article 1, meet all the requirements. Tell me, please, was the reason to establish the Central Military Prison in Heliodrom exactly as it is stated here in the statements of reason of this decision?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you have any information about who actually issued the decision about the establishment of the prison, who it was who decided to establish that prison at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't know who decided that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, in paragraph 8 of your statement you say that the Heliodrom Prison was to be used only for prisoners who breached the law, and, therefore, I'm going to ask you to look at P956, page 12, which is 14 in the English version of the document. Mr. Nikolic, have you got it?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We have plenty of time.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You said page 14?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, 12 in Croatian, 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you see a table here, and underneath it says: "In accordance with the Decree on the Treatment of Persons Imprisoned in Armed Conflicts, the head of the Defence Department approved the request of the Military Police Administration and, on the 3rd of September, 1992, issued a decision establishing the Central Military Prison in Mostar." My question to you, Mr. Nikolic, is this: Did you know that the Military Police Administration submitted a request to the head of the Defence Department for the establishment of a prison at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say that Mile Pusic was appointed commander. Now I'm interested in the following sentence: "In the Central Military Prison, all war detainees and prisoners are being sent -- all prisoners of war and detainees are sent to the CVZ, while prisoners who have committed misdemeanors or less serious criminal offences as well as detainees who have been given detention by the commanding authority are kept in military police company bases in military detention facilities during investigation." My question to you is this: From this military police report, it would follow that the Central Military Prison at Heliodrom was established in order to take in prisoners of war. Tell us, please, was Heliodrom for prisoners of war or not?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now, tell me, Mr. Nikolic, since you have had experience in the civilian prison system, if, in a barracks, you organise a military prison in which you -- which is designed to take in prisoners of war, that is to say, people belonging to an enemy army, do you have to take more stringent measures to keep the prisoners secure and keep them in an isolated place?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that question because I'm not a military expert. But if they were in a civilian prison, I would step up the guarding system and security system.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Nikolic, Ms. Tomasegovic showed you Milivoj Petkovic's order of the 24th of June about relocating the prison, because it was up at the front-line to begin with, so now let's look at the document again. It is P2925, and you have it in my binder as well. P2925 is the document number. And take a look in the "delivered to" sector. It was delivered to the Justice Department and the Department of the Interior. Tell us, please, Mr. Nikolic, in keeping with your knowledge of the way in which written communication was done in Herceg-Bosna, would it be logical to say that the Chief of the Main Staff sent this piece of information to these two departments because those two departments demanded the relocation of the prison from the front-line for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Madam Counsel, this is how it should have been done, but I should have been sent this document as well, as the protagonist for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Nikolic, I'm going to show you the testimony of Witness Zoran Buntic, and I'm going to refer to pages, for the record, 30617 and 30618. And I'm going to ask you, Mr. Nikolic, to listen to me and then tell me whether what I have read out is correct or not. And I'm going to quote the cross-examination conducted by Ms. Nozica, my colleague. Zoran Buntic gave an answer, saying that the prisoners from the civilian prison were transferred to Heliodrom in May 1993, after the conflict broke out between the Bosniaks and Croats in Mostar, and that that could have been between the 10th and 15th of the month. And then he said that in the Central Military Prison at Heliodrom, there existed a section which was a civilian prison and that that section was under the supervision of the warden of the civilian prison, and that he thinks that that person was Mr. Pero Nikolic. Now, when asked another question, whether he meant Pero Nikolic as the warden of this separate section in Heliodrom where the civilian inmates were put up, Zoran Buntic said: "Yes, I think that is right." Then he went on to say that those civilians were under the jurisdiction of the civilian legislative bodies. Now, tell me, Mr. Nikolic, this testimony by Mr. Zoran Buntic, is it correct, in your opinion, or not?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That completes my cross-examination, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Kruger. Mr. Kruger, you have one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honour, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom. If I may just have a lectern, please. And I do have a packet of exhibit. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, from your statement, the very last paragraph, paragraph 14, and from what you've said today, it would appear that you have known Mr. Josip Praljak for nearly 40 years now and you're on good terms with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And in all those years you've known him, you find him -- you trust him as a friend?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: He's a reliable person and a loyal person to you?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Have you always found him to be honest?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, you've also worked with him. I mean, you assigned him the task of supervising, for instance, the building of the prison in part of Heliodrom. Did you find him to be meticulous and precise in how he always performed his work?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you've said today that it's been 18 years since these events occurred that you're testifying about, and a number of times you said you can't remember, and sometimes you're not sure, and that's because you're just relying on your memory today and your memory isn't perfect, after 18 years, on exactly what happened 18 years ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you had written things down as they happened 18 years ago, do you think you would be more -- be able to provide more precise information to the Court today or you would have been able to provide more precise information to the Court today?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would, wherein it comes to dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, your friend, Mr. Praljak, he did precisely that. Do you think it's possible that his record that he provided in his diary may actually be more accurate than your memory is today?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't want to enter into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look at this, and then we'll come back to it again. Now, sir, in your statement, paragraph 12, you say: "I know for certain Mr. Josip Praljak was never a military policeman, and never in my life did I see him in a military police uniform or wearing a military police badge." Now, sir, let's see what Mr. Praljak actually testified on this. And for the transcript, I'm referring to his testimony on 26 February 2007, and it's at transcript page 14661, from line 19. And this was his evidence-in-chief. He said -- the question was by the Prosecutor: "As we move into 1993, and after Mr. Bozic returned, as we saw in the last document, at approximately the end of March, so we're focusing on that period forward, please, is it correct that under -- or at that time you," and this is now Mr. Praljak being referred to, "Mr. Bozic and Mr. Smiljanic were all HVO military police or did you consider yourself to be HVO police?" And Mr. Praljak answered: "Yes." And then he was asked again, a few pages further -- on the next page, transcript reference 14662 from line 18, the answer was: "In June, the 5th Battalion --" this is now Mr. Praljak speaking. He says: "In June, the 5th Battalion of the Military Police was established with Ivan Antic as commander. At that time, this prison where I, Bozic, Smiljanic, and the guard service worked became attached to one of the companies of that battalion as a security platoon. The commander of the company was Mr. Luka Sunjic." And then he was asked: "All right. Several questions about this. During this time and again following up on the questions asked by Judges earlier, did you, through Mr. Bozic, yourself --" "though," it says, "Mr. Bozic, yourself, Mr. Smiljanic, all continue to be members of the military police, and were you paid your salary from the military police throughout the war?" And again Mr. Praljak answered: "Yes." And then Mr. Praljak was cross-examined by counsel for Mr. Coric, and this was on the 1st of March, 2007. And the transcript reference, Your Honours, is transcript page 14936 from line 22. The question was: "Generally speaking, do you know whether military police was also engaged in combat on the front-line? I'm not speaking only about your experience in prison. You were a military policeman. Maybe you should know." And Mr. Praljak's answer to this was: "I don't know that because I never moved anywhere from Heliodrom." So now, sir, here's my question: From this, it seems that Mr. Praljak twice, to direct questions by the Prosecution, confirmed he was a member of the military police, and then the counsel for Mr. Coric actually also said, You were a military policeman, and he didn't deny it. So, sir, is it possible that Mr. Praljak is actually correct, in that he says he was a military policeman in 1993 or a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I claim today that I didn't see him wearing a military police uniform when he came to see me in the prison. Now, whether he was or was not, he is best placed to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: On the uniform -- let's have a look at that, and let's look at Mr. Praljak's answer to questions by the Judges. And this is on the 27th of February, 2007, transcript reference page 14732 from line 8. And Judge Mindua, he asked: "A short question, Witness. A moment ago, you said that Mr. Berislav Pusic was a member of the military police until July, when he became head of the Exchange Office. Now, what do you mean when you say 'member of the military police'? Was he a soldier in a uniform with a rank or not?" And then Mr. Praljak said: "While Berislav Pusic was a member of the military police, he wore a uniform, just like I did." I'll skip a line. And then Judge Antonetti asked: "You said he wore the same uniform as you. And what uniform was that?" "The Witness: It was a camouflage uniform of the military police, just like the other soldiers." Now, sir, if you say you never saw Mr. Praljak in a uniform, what you're saying by that is: You're not saying he never wore a military police uniform. According to his own evidence, he did. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So far as your statement would suggest that Mr. Praljak was not a military policeman and did not wear a military police uniform, it's not correct; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know for how long he wore a military police uniform and how long he was a military policeman for, but I know he was an administrator down there and that he was a candidate for the post of warden at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's actually turn back, then, to this meeting of the 8th of September, 1992. And this is the meeting which Mr. Praljak, Mr. Josip Praljak, writes about in his diary, and which he says took place between you and Mr. Coric and him in Ljubuski on the 8th of September, 1992. Now, sir, you've said that your memory is not perfect, but Mr. Praljak wrote down the things as they happened. Do you think it's likely that Mr. Praljak is actually correct when he says this meeting took place and that your memory simply failed you on this point?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Whether Josip Praljak went to see Mr. Valentin, I don't know that, I can't confirm that. But what I'm saying is that I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, let's go back to this document. And for this, if you open your binder, in the very first document it's Exhibit P00352. Now, this is the diary of Mr. Josip Praljak, and I've only extracted the three pages that I'm going to refer to. The full diary is in Ms. Tomasegovic's binder. If we look at the first page of this diary, and it's actually page 11 of the original, and this is once again that entry on the 7th of September, 1992. And you have it before you. And on the right of your page, sir, it's -- you're on the right page, sir. On the right, it says he is recording Mr. Praljak on the 7th of September: "Meeting with warden." Now, sir, if he says "Meeting with warden," do you agree he's referring to you as the warden of the Central Remand Prison or the Mostar Central Prison?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He would refer to me as warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And is it correct -- he testified, actually, when he was here that you and he would meet just about every day, and this was about the refurbishment of Heliodrom. Would you agree with that, in the mornings you met?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, here he says: "The warden informed me he had announced a meeting with Valentin Coric in Ljubuski." So, sir, you simply don't remember that this occurred, that you had set up a meeting with Mr. Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, he would have no reason to fabricate this piece of evidence in his diary 18 years ago?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can't really answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next page of the diary, page 12. This is the -- you're at the right page, sir.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This is the 8th of September, and Mr. Praljak records: "Meeting in Ljubuski with Chief Valentin Coric." He says: "In addition to the chief, the following were present: "Warden Pero Nikolic and Josip Praljak." And then he says: "At the start, the warden introduced me by name. Then he informed the chief that works are about to be finished and that moving in or transfer of military prisoners from the prison to Mostar can start ..." And then it goes on. The next bullet: "The chief informed us of the importance of military police and how it should be organised. He said that the prison at Heliodrom is the central military prison for Herceg-Bosna. As for prison warden, the most responsible man, who will be my very confidential person, I spoke to him and he agreed. He is Mile Pusic." And then at the bottom of that bullet point, it says: "You, Pero, designate guards, shift commanders, to get work going, and I will later appoint security commander. In 10 to 15 days, I will send directive on work in prison for each post and house rules to be strictly implemented. The move shall be carried out on 22 September 1992." So I put it to you that Mr. Praljak's memory on this and what he recorded here is actually accurate, that this occurred, even though you may not remember it.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I talked to Mr. Mile Pusic with respect to giving my guards for training, to train his guards, several guards, as professionals, to train them. But this was a meeting with Mijo Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: I would repeat my question to you from the previous page. This elaborate recording of a meeting, Mr. -- your friend, Mr. Praljak, he had no reason, 18 years ago, to fabricate such an elaborate piece or to lie about such a meeting; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I also don't have any reason to either deny or confirm something that I don't know happened. I don't gain anything or lose anything if I say anything but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Have a look at the next page of the document, and then we'll step off this. And this is page 13 of Exhibit P00352, and this is his entry for the 10th of September, just after the meeting with Mr. Praljak: "Briefing with warden. "Pero informed those present of the meeting held in Ljubuski, which, apart from me, was attended by Josip." So here is a third entry by Mr. Praljak on this meeting, and, sir, I put it to you that this meeting did take place and that you actually reported what occurred at that meeting to your subordinates. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I'd just like to say I don't know what it is in the English, but in the Croatian on this page there's something that's not quite clear, because this is Josip Praljak's diary and here it says that: "Pero informed those present about the meeting in Ljubuski, which, in addition to me, Josip attended." So from that, I can't see who the "I" is and who the "Josip" is, since there are two Josips. And according to Josip Praljak, there were four of them at the meeting, two Josips, one Coric, and one Pero. Perhaps the Prosecutor knows, because it's really not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take the point of Ms. Tomasegovic. I've had a look at the diary, and it would appear that the recordings by Mr. Praljak are virtually literal, that if somebody stated, I did this and that, it was actually recorded in the diary as: "I did this or that."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, just to be clear, then, I put it to you that when it says: "Pero informed those present of the meeting --" MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] No, he didn't say, I did this or that. On the page we saw earlier on from the meeting in Ljubuski, he writes that there were three people attending the meeting. According to him, there were Mr. Pero Nikolic, who's before us here, Mr. Josip Praljak, and Mr. Coric. Now, if we read this page, what he says is: "Pero informed," that means this gentleman here, "informed those present about the meeting in Ljubuski," the meeting held in Ljubuski, "which, in addition to me, was attended by Josip." Now, if we know that "Josip" is Josip Praljak, who is "in addition to me," who's the "I"? That's the part that's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would submit that from the English, it does appear clear to me that Pero is informing that "in addition to me, Pero, the meeting held in Ljubuski, suggesting with Mr. Coric, was also attended by Josip." To me, it's clear. I don't quite see the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, is it possible that your memory is wrong on this when the meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, look here. Counsel and Mr. Prosecutor, I wanted to say who this "Josip" was. If he wrote this diary, who is the Josip sitting next to him at the briefing in my office? So I'm is bit surprised. That one doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, let's move on, and I'll just find your statement. You say that in your statement, paragraph 8, in the middle: "I am certain that Valentin Coric was not in any way involved in these works." This is the refurbishment of Heliodrom to accommodate a prison. He was not in any way involved with these works, nor did he know of them. Now, sir, let's turn to Exhibit P00513 in your binder. 513, it's the third document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, I have a question. Mr. Kruger, I apologise, I have a question because I believe you want to move on to another document. If you plan to put this question afterwards, please interrupt me instantly. That won't be a problem. In this diary written by Josip Praljak, on the 10th of September, 1992, on the third line, we can read that the person in charge of the Heliodrom will be appointed according to a decision taken by the chief, Valentin Coric, the chief of the HVO military police, and the person in charge will be Mile Pusic. In a document P452, which we have seen a few moments ago, P452, a decision is taken here by Bruno Stojic, who sets up the military prison in the Heliodrom, precisely, and who appoints Mr. Mile Pusic in charge of the prison. There is seemingly a contradiction here in these documents. Could the witness correct me on this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I can't, because I don't know. I don't know who it was who appointed wardens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, before we look at document P00513, your statement says this, and you testified about this as well today: You said, in paragraph 7: "Despite my efforts, the conditions weren't good." And then: "A commission therefore met in the municipal Staff, and recognising that the prison was overcrowded, they requested that prisoners of war and detained members of the HVO and BH Army be relocated, and that the prison in Santic Street would therefore only be a civilian prison. And in a conversation with Mr. Mile Pusic, commander of the Krusevac Battalion which was based at Heliodrom, he gave the Municipal Staff permission for us to try and make a temporary military prison in one building and one or two [indiscernible] at Heliodrom." And that's what you testified today as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, from your testimony, it would appear that this whole idea of using Heliodrom or part of Heliodrom to accommodate prisoners of war, that that was something which was exclusively arranged between the Municipal Staff and Mr. Mile Pusic. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've already -- or let's have a look at document P00513. That's the document you have in front of you. And this is an order by Mr. Valentin Coric, and it's dated 22 September 1992. And we have had a look at it earlier today as well. He says -- he orders: "To establish a central military prison of the Croatian Defence Council in the barracks situated at Mostar Heliport." And then he says also: "The prison governor shall be responsible for the operation of the prison. "This order shall come into effect on 22 September ..." So, sir, in light of what you've just said, actually you're wrong, that it wasn't something that was arranged exclusively between Mr. Mile Pusic and the Municipal Council or Staff. From this, it's clear that Mr. Valentin Coric also had a role to play, he was also involved in this. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Objection, objection. In the statement, when the witness speaks about the role of municipal authorities and the role of Mr. Mile Pusic, he speaks about the period before any construction works took place. Therefore, the summer of 1992, and this document was created after that. And in his statement, the witness said that after the construction works were completed, he did not go to Heliodrom and he doesn't know how Heliodrom functioned once it was established as a prison. He didn't say who it was who established Heliodrom. He only said that somebody had an idea and there was a need to transfer prisoners, and then there were construction works, and all that preceded the document that we're looking at now and he wouldn't be able to say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness, himself, could have said, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But then let's step on. On this, Mr. Coric, obviously from this order, where he says, on 22 September, that this prison is established, I put it to you that he knew that the prison would be ready on the 22nd of September because he had been kept abreast of the refurbishment of the prison and he'd been kept abreast of it by people, such as yourself, who met with him on the 8th of September, 1992. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was not the one who kept him abreast of anything. I was not duty-bound to do so, because he was not my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But from this, you would agree that it does appear that Mr. Coric was aware that the prison was ready by the 22nd of September? You would agree to that?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can agree that he perhaps knew, or perhaps he didn't know. I can't say for certain either that he knew or that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: But, sir, that's not what you said in your statement. In your statement, you said: "I am certain that Valentin Coric was not involved, nor that he knew of these works." So now you're saying, actually, you're not certain?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am certain that I never told him anything, because I never saw him, I never sat down with him, he never sent me a letter, I never sent a letter back. That's what I am talking about. He could have known. He did not have to know. What sources he had at his disposal to learn about things, you have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, you've just been shown -- or you've just been referred by Judge Mindua to Exhibit P00452, and that's the decision by Mr. Bruno Stojic saying the central -- this is of the 3rd of September, 1992, and it says: "The Central Military Prison is hereby established in the Heliodrom barracks." And: "2. Mr. Mile Pusic from Krusevo-Mostar is hereby appointed warden of the Central Military Prison." Now, I further put it to you that Mr. Stojic and Mr. Coric's actions in setting up this prison are actually related; that Mr. Coric, his order to establish the prison on the 22nd, was actually preceded by this, and he was executing the decision by Mr. Stojic. Would you agree to that, or can you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I just prepared the facilities to house military personnel that would be criminally charged. I was not a factor to sit down with them on an equal footing and talk to them. I was just an official in a district prison in Mostar that was six kilometres away from there, and I really never had an opportunity to sit down with them. They're here. They can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in paragraph 13 you say: "I can safely assert that he," and this is now Mr. Praljak, "he never once mentioned to me that Valentin Coric had any role in appointing him or anyone else at Heliodrom." But, sir, the fact that he didn't mention it to you, that doesn't mean that it didn't happen. I put it to you that actually Mr. Coric did appoint wardens. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you just repeat your answer, sir? The interpreters didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Don't ask me whether he did or whether he didn't. I didn't make any decisions, I didn't hear. Why are you asking me if I know whether Mr. Coric appointed anybody? I was not in the same league. I was affiliated with the municipality, and the Heliodrom was a military prison. Why are you putting me in a context with all the other people who might have been in a position to know what Coric was doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, already twice today you've been shown Exhibit P02925, and that's the 24 June order by Mr. Petkovic. And we don't need to look at it. I'm just going to ask you a question about this. This is the order where Mr. Petkovic orders that all prisoners shall be transferred to the Heliodrom military remand facility. Now, sir, this order, if I read it correctly, that means that the prisoners remaining in your prison, and these were the civilian criminals, as it were, that these people were transferred to the Heliodrom Military Prison; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At the Heliodrom military remand facility, did you and your staff also get transferred there to work there or not?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I never went back to Heliodrom once it was established. None of my guards were transferred to Heliodrom either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, do you know whether those prisoners, those civilian prisoners, when they were transferred to Heliodrom, were they kept separate from the other detainees in Dretelj or kept in amongst them?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. I wasn't down there and I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just a final thing perhaps. Along with these prisoners who were sent, the civilian prisoners, were they only male prisoners or were there also women amongst them?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Only men, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And were they of any particular ethnic grouping?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It really doesn't matter. I don't know what their ethnicity was. I know that there were quite a number of Croats. There were Muslims as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in 1992, you testified that Serbian prisoners of war were also being held in your facility. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And these are the prisoners who were then later sent to Heliodrom when it was established on 22 September 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of Serbian prisoners of war being detained in any other locations - example, Dretelj - in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I heard of that, but I never went to Dretelj. I don't know, to this very day, where that is or where that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, from this it would appear that in 1993, when the HVO detained large numbers of Muslim men, this wasn't the first experience they had of detaining people; they had gained experience of detaining prisoners of war already in 1992. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know who you mean. What type? I don't understand your question, sir. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In 1993, when the HVO was detaining large numbers of Muslim men, and these included military men as well as, actually, civilian military-aged men, conscripts, that wasn't the first experience they had of detaining such people, because they'd already gained some experience in 1992 of detaining Serbian prisoners of war; is that correct? You don't disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't agree, for a very simple reason. Nobody came to me in mid-1992. None of the Muslims were detained there, and those who were brought in before that, they came in on decisions for custody from either a civilian judge or a military judge, depending on their status. That's how people ended up in my prison. As far as mass arrests are concerned, I did not receive any of them as a result of any mass arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to know whether the Coric Defence has some redirect questions. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will need only five minutes, without any documents. Maybe we could do that before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sure, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, if I understood you properly, you godfathered Mr. Josip Praljak's children, you were a good friend with him. Being a godfather is a big thing in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: This event, you coming to testify before the Tribunal, is that an important event in your life, an unusual event?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell your friends, your relatives, that you were on your way to The Hague to testify?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I told only my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Praljak had testified here in The Hague? Did you know that before you arrived here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I learned that at the wedding two months ago. He only told me, I was in The Hague. There were over 500 guests at the wedding. He didn't have much time. He greeted me as one of the wedding festivity's participants and thanked me for being there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you surprised to hear that he had been in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, you were asked about that meeting, and you were asked about what you remembered. And if I understood your answers properly, your recollection is problematic in the part in which -- you actually don't remember dates very well, but you remember the events. Did I understand that properly?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as you sit here today, can you state with certainty -- or, rather, let me put it differently. Did you ever attend a single meeting with Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you 100 per cent sure that you never, ever met with Mr. Valentin Coric?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I asked you whether you were 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Listen to my question. Don't rush into answering, please. I'm going to repeat my question. You answer it very slowly. After you've heard my question, count before you answer. Are you 100 per cent sure that never, ever in your life did you ever meet with Mr. Valentin Coric? Are you 100 per cent sure of that?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent, I'm sure that I have never had the honour of sharing the same table or sit down with Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, sir : The civilians you mentioned as having been transferred from your prison, you've already talked about that, but let's just go over the same ground once again. Were those civilians who were undergoing investigation because of crimes that they had committed?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: Those are the civilians that had been brought on decision of investigating judge by the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: PERO NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That completes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for coming to testify for Mr. Coric's Defence, and I would like to wish you a safe trip back to your country. Before we adjourn for the day, I would like to let you know that next week we have a witness that will testify over four days. I would like to ask Mr. Coric's counsel if there won't be a problem and if he will definitely be here. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if everything goes smoothly, he should be landing just as we speak. Around half past 10.00, his flight should land, so I suppose everything will be fine. We spoke to him yesterday evening. He confirmed his arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning to each of Your Honours, to all those in and around the courtroom. One procedural matter, please. And I didn't want to delay the beginning of the witness at 9.00. But in connection with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Perhaps the witness will be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday, in connection with the testimony of Mr. Petkovic, lengthy objections were filed by the various Defence teams to the Prosecution's tendered exhibits. I think there was something like 27 pages of objections. Frankly, it was impossible for us to respond by this morning, and I would ask the Chamber if we could have until close of business next Wednesday to possibly submit those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. May I say we have absolutely no objection to that. We wonder whether there could be a general extension for everybody to the same dead-line. That makes sense. We've done that in the past, and Your Honours may feel that that's fair and reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, the Trial Chamber agrees with that. There is no problem. It is quite understandable that when there's a lot of work involved, we give enough time for everyone to prepare themselves. Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be brief. Yesterday, at one point I requested time to consult with my counsel, and you did not even react. You kept quiet to that. I just want to tell you one fact. For the four years of this trial and over 500 sessions in this courtroom, I requested that for the second or third time. It doesn't matter. Next time, if I request that, and if I'm entitled to that, would you please allow that to happen within a reasonable time or at the moment when I requested it? I had a good reason yesterday, because I'd noticed that something was happening to the witness, that he was not feeling too good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Mr. Coric, I had taken your request on board, and I thought that during the break you would have time to consult with your counsel. But then you left, and I realised that the co-counsel was no longer there, so I assumed that you were consulting. This is why I did not insist on that, and your counsel is telling me that, indeed, the co-counsel met with you. But next time there won't be any problem. You can, of course, consult with your counsel. This being said, we will meet again on Monday at 2.15 p.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 29th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: [The Accused Praljak and Pusic not present]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.39 a.m.,
